title: The water was already at his chest.
paragraphs: The water was already at his chest.

Wind screaming.
Waves collapsing.
The boat shrinking in the distance.
And Peter—the fisherman who knew these waters better than anyone—was losing the fight.
One moment earlier, he had done the impossible.
He stepped out of the boat.
Let that sink in.
While the other disciples clung to the wood in fear, Peter climbed over the edge and put his foot on the sea.
And for a moment…
He walked.

Not because Peter was powerful.
Not because his faith was flawless.
But because his eyes were locked on Jesus.
Matthew tells us something chilling and human at the same time:
“But when he saw the wind, he was afraid, and beginning to sink he cried out, ‘Lord, save me.’” (Matthew 14:30)
Notice the order.

Fear.
Then sinking.
Peter didn’t jump into the water.
He began to sink.
That’s how spiritual collapse often works.

No one wakes up planning to drown in doubt, sin, anxiety, or shame.
It starts small.

A glance away from Christ.
A moment of fear louder than faith.
A storm that suddenly looks bigger than the Savior.
Peter saw the wind.
Not Jesus.
And when the storm filled his vision, the water started pulling him down.
Sound familiar?
Maybe you started your journey with Jesus boldly.
You stepped out of the boat.

You trusted Him.
You prayed with fire.
You believed His promises.
But then the winds came.

Bills piled up.
A relationship broke apart.
Temptation crept back.
The anxiety returned.
The silence of unanswered prayers started to feel heavy.
And suddenly the waves look massive.
Your faith begins to wobble.
Your heart whispers the same fear Peter felt:
“I’m going under.”
But this moment in Matthew 14 is not a story about Peter’s failure.
It’s a story about Jesus’ grip.
Scripture says:
“Immediately Jesus reached out his hand and caught him.” (Matthew 14:31)
Immediately.
No hesitation.
No delay.

Jesus didn’t wait for Peter to fix himself.
He didn’t wait for Peter to swim harder.
He didn’t say, “Prove your faith first.”
Peter cried three desperate words:
“Lord, save me.”
And heaven moved.
This is the Gospel in miniature.
We are Peter.

We step out in faith… then tremble.
We believe… then doubt.
We follow Christ… then suddenly see the wind.

Sin sinks us.
Fear sinks us.
Pride sinks us.
Shame sinks us.
And if salvation depended on how tightly we hold onto Jesus…
We would all drown.
But the good news of the Gospel is this:
Our salvation is not secured by our grip on Christ.
It is secured by His grip on us.
That hand that grabbed Peter in the storm…
Is the same hand that would soon be pierced by Roman nails on the cross.
Jesus did not come merely to teach us how to stay afloat.
He came to rescue drowning sinners.
On the cross, Christ stepped into the deepest storm of all—our sin, our guilt, our judgment.
The waves of wrath that should have swallowed us… fell on Him.
Three days later, He rose from the grave, proving that sin, death, and the storm itself do not have the final word.
That means if you are sinking today…
You are not beyond rescue.

Your fear does not disqualify you.
Your doubt does not shock Him.
Your weakness does not repel Him.
The Savior who walked on the water still walks into storms.
And He still reaches for people who cry out.
Maybe that is you today.
Maybe your faith feels thin.
Maybe your life feels like waves crashing over your head.
Maybe you are exhausted from trying to keep yourself afloat.
Listen carefully.
Peter didn’t pray a long religious prayer.
He didn’t quote theology.
He simply cried:
“Lord, save me.”
Three words.
And Jesus answered.
If your heart is drowning in guilt, shame, addiction, fear, or despair—cry out to Him.
Jesus Christ is still saving sinners.
Not because we are strong.
But because He is.
So lift your eyes again.
Not to the wind.
Not to the waves.
To the One standing above them.
And remember this truth that storms cannot erase:

The hand that holds you
is stronger than the storm that scares you.

“Immediately Jesus reached out His hand and caught him.”
— Matthew 14:31
Someone in your life might be sinking right now—and they need to know the Savior still reaches.
Because Jesus still saves.
